 Changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) included in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) mean that some older adults now find themselves subject to work requirements in order to qualify.
 Lisa Reese is one of them.

 Reese, who lives in Capitol Heights, Maryland, in a home that belonged to her grandparents, told NPR that she chose to retire at 62 so that she could care for her family members.

 When her Social Security wasn’t enough to get by on, she applied for SNAP benefits, qualifying for $63 a month. But to get them, she has to meet an 80-hour a month work requirement.
 ‘I decided to retire to take care of everybody’
 Reese told NPR that prior to retiring, she’d never received government assistance. She worked for nearly 40 years in retail, as a cleaner and in the hospitality industry, including 25 years at Marriott.
 She said that caring for family was the biggest factor in her decision to retire; her 80-year-old mother is in senior living, and her uncle, who shares the Capitol Heights home, had cancer surgery. Reese’s daughter and 2-year-old granddaughter also live in the home.
 “Daycare was expensive,” Reese told NPR. “So I decided to retire to take care of everybody. I don’t know if that’s crazy.”
 But Reese said that managing the cost of living on Social Security was difficult, especially with rising prices, including a gas bill that “went through the roof,” she told NPR. “One of my bills was $500. Five hundred!”
 Reese said her efforts — cutting spending, adhering to a strict budget and using a local food bank — weren’t enough, and she applied for SNAP this summer.

 Work requirements
 OBBBA changes to SNAP mean that adults aged 55 to 64 are now subject to time limit work requirements, meaning they must work, volunteer or participate in training for at least 80 hours a month.

 The OBBBA also ended exemptions from work requirements for people experiencing homelessness, veterans and individuals ages 18 to 24 who have aged out of foster care.
 According to an estimate from the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, based on United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) data, from July 2025 to July 2026, 5.5 million fewer people received SNAP benefits.
 To meet her 80-hour requirement, Reese volunteers at Mission of Love Charities, which operates a food pantry, and provides other assistance to low-income individuals and people experiencing homelessness, including helping people apply for SNAP benefits.
 The Mission’s CEO, Adenia Bradley, told NPR that the nonprofit is seeing the impacts of SNAP requirements first-hand. “We see it every day, people get cut off,” Bradley told NPR, saying that it can be for small errors, red tape or work requirements.
 A White House spokesperson told NPR that SNAP’s “mission to be temporary help for those in tough times was a total failure,” stating that the OBBBA’s changes “began the process to halt fraud and ensure that it only serves eligible Americans who need it most.”
 Reese told NPR that she thinks SNAP should only be for temporary use. “The ones that’s been on it for 10, 15, 20 years, yeah, they do need to get off of it. It’s hurting folks like me,” she said. “I’m sorry if that sounds cruel. But go after them, not the retirees.”
 Who gets SNAP benefits?
 According to a report from The Hamilton Project, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data from 2023 show that about 35% of SNAP participants were children, and 15% were people 65 and older. Of working-age SNAP participants (ages 18 to 64), 34% had dependents under 18, and 22% were students or people with a disability.

 h2]:mt-8 [&>h2]:lg:mt-12 [&>h2]:mb-4 [&>h2]:lg:mb-6">
 A USDA report from 2025, using 2023 data, found that most households receiving SNAP benefits “included a child, an elderly individual or a non-elderly individual with a disability. [And 79%] of households — which contained [88%] of all participants — included at least one of these individuals.”
 The report says 83% of all SNAP benefits, excluding emergency allotments, went to these households.
 A 2020 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report prepared for the U.S. Senate Committee On The Budget found that about 70% of wage-earning adults in households that received Medicaid and SNAP worked full-time hours. It also found that 72% of wage-earning adults receiving SNAP and Medicaid were employed “in the five industries with the highest concentrations of low-wage workers.”
 Nine states provided employer data on SNAP recipients, and in seven of those nine states, “restaurants (and other eating places) employed the largest percentage of working adult SNAP
 recipients,” the report says.

 “Department stores, grocery stores, employment services agencies and general merchandise stores (e.g., box and discount stores) also featured prominently in these states.”
 The report included rankings of the 25 employers with the largest estimated number of SNAP recipients for each of the nine states reporting employer data — Arkansas, Georgia, Indiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Nebraska, North Carolina, Tennessee and Washington.
 Walmart was the No. 1 employer of SNAP recipients for five states, No. 2 in three states and the No. 4 employer of SNAP recipients in Massachusetts.
 McDonald’s was also included in all nine states’ rankings; it was the No. 1 employer of SNAP recipients in Nebraska, and No. 2 in four other states.
 Walmart’s net profit in 2025 was $19.44 billion; McDonald’s was $8.563 billion.
